section.title: Parables, the Storm, and Jairus
section.sectionRationale: This movement gathers Jesus' teaching about the word and a chain of mighty acts that show His authority. He preaches the kingdom with women supporting Him, tells the parable of the sower and explains it, adds the lamp and His true family, then displays His power over nature, demons, disease, and death: calming the storm, freeing the Gerasene demoniac, healing the bleeding woman, and raising Jairus' daughter. The word planted in the heart and the Lord who commands even wind and death belong together.
section.thesis: The word of God is the seed that saves those who hear it with a good heart and hold on to it, and the One who sows that word is the Lord whose bare command stills the storm, casts out Legion, heals the incurable, and raises the dead, so that faith in Him is met by His saving power.
section.frameNote: Six movements: the women who supported Jesus; the parable of the sower and its meaning; the lamp and Jesus' true family; the calming of the storm; the deliverance of the Gerasene demoniac; and the healing of the bleeding woman with the raising of Jairus' daughter.

units.label: The women who followed
units.note: supporting the mission out of their own means

verses.text: Soon afterward, Jesus traveled from one town and village to another, preaching and proclaiming the good news of the {{basileia|kingdom}} of God. The Twelve were with Him,
as well as some women who had been healed of evil spirits and infirmities: Mary called Magdalene, from whom seven demons had gone out,
Joanna the wife of Herod’s household manager Chuza, Susanna, and many others. These women were ministering to them out of their own means.

units.label: The parable of the sower
units.note: the seed is the word of God

verses.text: While a large crowd was gathering and people were coming to Jesus from town after town, He told them this parable:
“A farmer went out to sow his seed. And as he was sowing, some seed fell along the path, where it was trampled, and the birds of the air devoured it.
Some fell on rocky ground, and when it came up, the seedlings withered because they had no moisture.
Other seed fell among thorns, which grew up with it and choked the seedlings.
Still other seed fell on good soil, where it sprang up and produced a crop, a hundredfold.” As Jesus said this, He called out, “He who has ears to hear, let him hear.”
Then His disciples asked Him what this parable meant.

He replied, “The knowledge of the mysteries of the kingdom of God has been given to you, but to others I speak in parables, so that, ‘though seeing, they may not see; though hearing, they may not understand.’
Now this is the meaning of the parable: The seed is the {{logos|word}} of God.
The seeds along the path are those who hear, but the devil comes and takes away the word from their hearts, so that they may not believe and be saved.
The seeds on rocky ground are those who hear the word and receive it with joy, but they have no root. They believe for a season, but in the time of testing, they fall away.
The seeds that fell among the thorns are those who hear, but as they go on their way, they are choked by the worries, riches, and pleasures of this life, and their fruit does not mature.
But the seeds on good soil are those with a noble and good heart, who hear the word, cling to it, and by persevering produce a crop.

units.label: The lamp and Jesus' true family
units.note: hearing the word of God and carrying it out

verses.text: No one lights a lamp and covers it with a jar or puts it under a bed. Instead, he sets it on a stand, so those who enter can see the light.
For there is nothing hidden that will not be disclosed, and nothing concealed that will not be made known and brought to light.
Pay attention, therefore, to how you listen. Whoever has will be given more, but whoever does not have, even what he thinks he has will be taken away from him.”
Then Jesus’ mother and brothers came to see Him, but they were unable to reach Him because of the crowd.
He was told, “Your mother and brothers are standing outside, wanting to see You.”
But He replied, “My mother and brothers are those who hear the word of God and carry it out.”

units.label: The calming of the storm
units.note: who is this? even wind and water obey Him

verses.text: One day Jesus said to His disciples, “Let us cross to the other side of the lake.” So He got into a boat with them and set out.
As they sailed, He fell asleep, and a windstorm came down on the lake, so that the boat was being swamped, and they were in great danger.
The disciples went and woke Him, saying, “Master, Master, we are perishing!” Then Jesus got up and rebuked the wind and the raging waters, and they subsided, and all was calm.
“Where is your {{pistis|faith}}?” He asked. Frightened and amazed, they asked one another, “Who is this? He commands even the winds and the water, and they obey Him!”

units.label: The Gerasene demoniac
units.note: Legion cast out, a man restored

verses.text: Then they sailed to the region of the Gerasenes, across the lake from Galilee.
When Jesus stepped ashore, He was met by a demon-possessed man from the town. For a long time this man had not worn clothing or lived in a house, but he stayed in the tombs.
When the man saw Jesus, he cried out and fell down before Him, shouting in a loud voice, “What do You want with me, Jesus, Son of the Most High God? I beg You not to torture me!”

For Jesus had commanded the unclean spirit to come out of the man. Many times it had seized him, and though he was bound with chains and shackles, he had broken the chains and been driven by the demon into solitary places.
“What is your name?” Jesus asked. “Legion,” he replied, because many demons had gone into him.
And the demons kept begging Jesus not to order them to go into the Abyss.
There on the hillside a large herd of pigs was feeding. So the demons begged Jesus to let them enter the pigs, and He gave them permission.
Then the demons came out of the man and went into the pigs, and the herd rushed down the steep bank into the lake and was drowned.
When those tending the pigs saw what had happened, they ran off and reported this in the town and countryside.
So the people went out to see what had happened. They came to Jesus and found the man whom the demons had left, sitting at Jesus’ feet, clothed and in his right mind; and they were afraid.
Meanwhile, those who had seen it reported how the demon-possessed man had been healed.
Then all the people of the region of the Gerasenes asked Jesus to depart from them, because great fear had taken hold of them. So He got into the boat and started back.
The man whom the demons had left begged to go with Jesus. But He sent him away, saying,
“Return home and describe how much God has done for you.” So the man went away and proclaimed all over the town how much Jesus had done for him.

units.label: The bleeding woman and Jairus' daughter
units.note: do not be afraid, only believe

verses.text: When Jesus returned, the crowd welcomed Him, for they had all been waiting for Him.
Just then a synagogue leader named Jairus came and fell at Jesus’ feet. He begged Him to come to his house,
because his only daughter, who was about twelve, was dying. As Jesus went with him, the crowds pressed around Him,
including a woman who had suffered from bleeding for twelve years. She had spent all her money on physicians, but no one was able to heal her.
She came up behind Jesus and touched the fringe of His cloak, and immediately her bleeding stopped.
“Who touched Me?” Jesus asked. But they all denied it. “Master,” said Peter, “the people are crowding and pressing against You.”
But Jesus declared, “Someone touched Me, for I know that power has gone out from Me.”

Then the woman, seeing that she could not escape notice, came trembling and fell down before Him. In the presence of all the people, she explained why she had touched Him and how she had immediately been healed.
“Daughter,” said Jesus, “your faith has {{sozo|healed}} you. Go in peace.”
While He was still speaking, someone arrived from the house of the synagogue leader. “Your daughter is dead,” he told Jairus. “Do not bother the Teacher anymore.”
But Jesus overheard them and said to Jairus, “Do not be afraid; just believe, and she will be healed.”
When He entered the house, He did not allow anyone to go in with Him except Peter, John, James, and the child’s father and mother.
Meanwhile, everyone was weeping and mourning for her. But Jesus said, “Stop weeping; she is not dead but asleep.”
And they laughed at Him, knowing that she was dead.
But Jesus took her by the hand and called out, “Child, get up!”
Her spirit returned, and at once she got up. And He directed that she be given something to eat.
Her parents were astounded, but Jesus ordered them not to tell anyone what had happened.

basileia.gloss: Kingdom, reign, the active rule of God breaking into the world. It is the good news Jesus proclaims from town to town and the mystery whose secrets are given to His disciples. The kingdom advances not by force but by the sown word taking root in receptive hearts, and by the King's authority over storm, demon, disease, and death.

logos.gloss: Word, message, the spoken revelation of God. In the parable the seed is the logos of God, the very message Jesus preaches. Its fruitfulness depends not on the seed, which is good, but on the soil of the heart that receives it; the good heart hears the word, clings to it, and by perseverance bears a crop.

pistis.gloss: Faith, trust that takes God at His word. In the storm Jesus asks, 'Where is your faith?', exposing how quickly fear crowds it out even in those who follow Him. Across this movement faith is the empty hand that reaches to Jesus, whether a woman touching His cloak or a father told simply to believe.

sozo.gloss: To save, heal, rescue, make whole. It spans the healing of the body and the salvation of the whole person. Jesus tells the bleeding woman, 'Your faith has saved you,' rendered here 'healed you,' and uses the same word of Jairus' daughter, 'she will be saved.' The wholeness Jesus gives reaches beyond the body to the person.

basic.context: Jesus travels preaching the kingdom, supported by women He had healed. He tells the parable of the sower: the same word falls on four kinds of heart, and only the good heart hears, holds on, and bears fruit. He adds that a lamp is meant to give light and that His true family are those who hear God's word and do it. Then Luke stacks four demonstrations of His authority. He calms a deadly storm with a word, delivers a man ruled by a legion of demons, heals a woman who had bled for twelve years the instant she touches His cloak, and raises Jairus' twelve-year-old daughter from death. The word must take root, and the One who sows it is Lord over everything that threatens us.
basic.hermeneutics: The sower is about the hearers, not the seed: the word is always good, but hearts differ, and only perseverance proves the good soil. The four miracles are arranged to answer the disciples' question in the boat, 'Who is this?' Nature, demons, chronic disease, and death all yield to Him. Faith runs through the section, from the disciples who lose it in the storm to the woman and the father who cast themselves on Jesus.
basic.originalLanguages: Jesus proclaims the basileia, the kingdom, whose secrets are given to His disciples and whose growth depends on the sown logos, the word of God, taking root in a good heart. In the storm He asks, 'Where is your pistis, your faith?' And to the bleeding woman He says her faith has sozo, saved and healed her, the same word He uses of Jairus' daughter.
basic.typology: Jesus stilling the sea recalls the God of the Psalms who rules the raging waters and rescues the perishing. Raising Jairus' daughter with 'Child, get up' anticipates His own resurrection and the final raising of all who belong to Him. The word as seed picks up Isaiah's promise that God's word will not return empty but accomplish His purpose.
basic.christ: The disciples' cry, 'Who is this? Even wind and water obey Him,' is the question the whole movement answers. Jesus does what only God can do: He commands the sea, masters a legion of demons, heals the incurable, and calls the dead back to life. He is the sower of the word and the Lord of the kingdom, and faith in Him is never disappointed.
basic.god: God's rule is breaking in through Jesus, and it comes by His word taking root in humble hearts. He is the God whose power over chaos, evil, sickness, and death is total, and who nonetheless stoops to a frightened woman and a grieving father. What He asks in return is faith: do not be afraid, only believe.
basic.crossReferences: Isaiah 55 promises that God's word will not return empty. Psalm 107 pictures the Lord who stills the storm and delivers the perishing. Isaiah 6 stands behind the parable's warning about seeing yet not seeing. And Luke 24 shows the resurrection to which the raising of Jairus' daughter points.
basic.oneStory: The kingdom advances as the word is sown and takes root, and the King reveals Himself as Lord over storm, demons, disease, and death. Scripture had promised a God whose word accomplishes His will and whose power rescues the perishing. In Jesus that God has drawn near, sowing the word and answering faith with saving power, all the way to raising the dead.

context.literary:
Luke 8 is a chapter about hearing, and it is built so that the opening teaching is tested by the closing miracles. The first half, verses 1 to 21, is about the word: the women who have heard and now serve, the sower, the lamp, and the family of those who 'hear the word of God and carry it out.' The second half, verses 22 to 56, is about the Word's Lord: four scenes in which something that no one could master, a storm, a legion, a twelve-year disease and death, bows to Him. Luke has set the parable of the sower at the head of the chapter so that the reader will watch for the four kinds of response in the scenes that follow.

The miracles are arranged as a staircase. The storm threatens the disciples' lives. The Gerasene man is held by a power that chains cannot hold. The woman has been ruined by a condition that physicians could not cure, and the girl is past all human help. Each scene reaches further from ordinary control than the last, and each ends in the same way, with fear. The disciples are 'frightened and amazed,' verse 25. The Gerasenes are 'afraid,' verses 35 and 37. The woman comes 'trembling,' verse 47. The mourners laugh at Him in verse 53, and the parents are 'astounded' in verse 56. Faith is never exactly the opposite of fear in Luke 8, since it is always found in the middle of it: 'Do not be afraid; just believe,' verse 50.

There is a deliberate interleaving in verses 40 to 56. Luke starts the story of Jairus, breaks off to tell of the woman, and then returns, so that the two accounts illuminate one another. The number twelve binds them: the woman has been bleeding for twelve years, and the girl is about twelve. One has been dying slowly as long as the other has been living. Both are called 'daughter,' and both are saved by faith, which is the one thing in the chapter that crosses from the woman to the father when the news arrives.

Notice too the little frame around the miracles. The chapter begins with the Twelve and the women sharing His journey, and ends with Jesus bidding the parents tell no one. Between them Luke keeps asking, in different voices, the question the boat asked: who is this?
context.historical:
The women of verses 2 and 3 are a quiet detail with a large meaning. Rabbis in the first century were not normally followed and funded by women. Luke names three: Mary from Magdala, Joanna, the wife of Chuza, who managed Herod Antipas's household, and Susanna. Joanna's husband worked inside the court of the very ruler who would later mock Jesus, and her support came from within that household. These women 'were ministering to them out of their own means,' and they stay faithful to the end, standing at a distance at the cross, Luke 23:49, and bringing the news from the empty tomb, Luke 24:10.

The Sea of Galilee lies in a basin about two hundred metres below sea level, ringed by hills, and cold air funnelling down from them can whip the surface into violent waves with very little warning. Several of the disciples were fishermen who knew these waters, which makes their panic more telling. They had met storms before, and this one was beyond what their skill could manage.

The east shore, the land of the Gerasenes, was largely Gentile. The place is a collision of uncleanness from a Jewish point of view: a foreign shore, tombs, a naked man, unclean spirits, and a herd of pigs. The name of the region varies in the manuscripts, with Gerasenes, Gadarenes and Gergesenes all attested, which probably reflects the fact that Gentile towns were scattered along that coast. 'Legion' was a Latin term, borrowed into Greek, for a Roman army unit of several thousand, and in an occupied country the word carried a sharp edge. The 'Abyss' of verse 31 is the place of confinement for evil spirits that Revelation 20:3 describes.

Jairus is an archisynagōgos, the lay head of a synagogue, responsible for organising worship and caring for the building. A man of standing falling at the feet of an itinerant teacher was a cost to his pride. The bleeding woman's condition fell under Leviticus 15:25 to 27, which made her ceremonially unclean and, by touch, others too, so for twelve years she had been shut out of ordinary worship and probably of ordinary life. She touches the 'fringe,' the tassel Israelites were to wear on their garments, Numbers 15:38 to 39. Mourning customs for a dead child usually involved hired flute players and wailers, so the crowd was already in place.
context.canonical:
The word of God as seed and as a power that cannot fail runs through the Old Testament. Isaiah 55:10 to 11 compares God's word to rain and snow that water the earth and provide 'seed to sow and food to eat,' and says it 'will not return to Me empty, but it will accomplish what I please.' Jesus' parable is Isaiah's image turned into a question about what the soil will do. The explanation in verse 10 quotes Isaiah 6:9 to 10, the commission to a prophet whose preaching hardens many. Both Isaiah and Jesus describe the same sad fact, that hearing can fail to become understanding. The other Gospels give the same parable, Matthew 13 and Mark 4, and the apostles later describe the word as a seed that gives new birth, 1 Peter 1:23, and a message that must be done, not merely heard, James 1:22. In Acts the word 'continued to spread,' Acts 6:7, which is the harvest of Luke 8:8.

The 'mysteries' of verse 10 belong to a biblical vocabulary running back to Daniel, who told Nebuchadnezzar that 'there is a God in heaven who reveals mysteries,' Daniel 2:28. A mystery in the Bible is not a puzzle but a truth that God discloses to those He chooses.

The storm scene belongs to a Psalm tradition about God's rule over the sea. 'You rule the raging sea; when its waves mount up, You still them,' Psalm 89:9. Psalm 107:23 to 30 pictures sailors terrified in a tempest who cry out, and the LORD 'calmed the storm to a whisper.' Psalm 65:7 places the stilling of the waves alongside the quieting of the nations. The scene of a sleeping figure in a storm-tossed boat also recalls Jonah, with a telling contrast: Jonah slept because he was running from God, and Jesus sleeps because He rests in the Father's care.

Elijah and Elisha raised children, 1 Kings 17 and 2 Kings 4, and Luke has already placed one raising at Nain. The raising of Jairus' daughter belongs in that line but exceeds it. The parallel accounts are in Mark 5 and Matthew 9. After the resurrection of Jesus, Peter raises Tabitha with words very like these, Acts 9:40, and the apostles' ministry follows the same pattern.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
Luke meant his readers to learn how to hear. 'Pay attention, therefore, to how you listen,' verse 18, is the sentence the whole chapter builds toward, and it is an instruction to anyone reading the Gospel. The word of the kingdom arrives in a world with enemies, hardships and distractions, and Luke wanted readers who had received it to examine their own soil and not assume that the first welcome is the same as endurance.

He also meant them to take comfort. The people who followed Jesus included frightened fishermen, a naked and chained man, a woman worn out by her condition and a father who watched his daughter die. Luke places the hard cases next to the Lord of the hard cases. A reader who is in a storm, or ashamed, or bereaved, is invited to see that Jesus is neither far away nor outmatched.

The movement of the chapter also carries a challenge about response. The Gerasenes asked Jesus to leave, the crowd laughed at Him, and the disciples took a while to understand who they were with. Luke does not hide that the reaction to Jesus' power is often fear and rejection. What he holds up as the good response is the quiet one of the healed man proclaiming 'how much Jesus had done for him,' verse 39, the woman telling her whole story, and the father who believes when all evidence is against it.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The chapter describes what Jesus did and what various people did in reply; it does not hand us a method. The sower is not asking us to turn ourselves into better soil by effort. The instruction 'Pay attention to how you listen' is a real command, but the parable is also a diagnostic: it shows what happens when the word meets hardness, shallowness, distraction and an honest heart, and it invites us to ask which description fits us.

Where readers have to be careful is in the miracles. That Jesus calmed a storm does not mean that every storm will be calmed, and that He raised a girl does not mean every child will be raised. These are signs of who He is. The abiding teaching is His authority and His care, not a guarantee against loss. Nor should the story of the pigs be turned into a general rule about demons and animals. The same applies to the woman's way of touching the fringe: her faith is commended, not her technique. What we are meant to copy is the trust that reaches for Him, and the boldness to tell the truth in public afterwards.

debates.question: Do the rocky and thorny soils describe people who were truly saved and then lost?

views.label: They were never truly rooted
views.case: Jesus says the rocky-ground hearers 'believe for a season' but have no root and fall away in testing, and only the good soil perseveres and bears fruit; genuine, saving reception is shown by lasting fruit, so the others had a temporary, rootless response.

views.label: A warning about real dangers to real hearers
views.case: Others stress the pastoral force: the soils warn every hearer that the devil, shallow enthusiasm, and the choking cares of life can rob the word of fruit, calling us to guard our hearing rather than to settle debates about who was 'really' saved.

debates.bearing: Either way the point stands: true hearing endures and bears fruit, so we are to receive the word with a good heart, cling to it, and persevere through testing and the cares of life.

debates.question: Why did Jesus insist on knowing who touched Him when the crowd was pressing all around?

views.label: To bring the woman's faith into the open
views.case: The healing was real the moment she touched Him, but Jesus draws her out so her secret, trembling faith becomes a public confession, and He can call her 'Daughter' and send her away in peace rather than leave her hiding in the crowd.

views.label: To distinguish faith from mere contact
views.case: Many were pressing against Jesus, but only one touched Him in faith; His question marks the difference between crowding near Him and actually trusting Him, honoring her faith before all.

debates.bearing: Both show that Jesus is not content with anonymous, magical contact; He seeks personal, confessed faith and gives the healed woman assurance and peace.

study.originalLanguages:
The parable's key terms are chosen with care. The seed that lands on good soil is said to be held by those with a kalē kai agathē kardia, a 'noble and good heart,' verse 15, an expression the Greeks used of moral excellence. Luke takes the phrase and gives it a new content: the good heart is the one that hears the word, katechousin, 'holds it fast,' and bears fruit en hypomonē, with endurance. The verb for holding fast is a strong one, as of keeping a grip on something that others will try to snatch. In verse 13 the rocky soil is described by the opposite: they 'receive' the word with joy but 'have no root,' ou echousin. The difference between the two is not the speed of the welcome but the staying power. Verse 18 then turns the whole parable into an instruction with the sharp imperative blepete pōs akouete, 'see how you hear.'

Luke records that the secrets of the kingdom are called mystēria, 'mysteries,' in verse 10, a plural that the Old Testament prepared for in Daniel 2. And he calls the lesson a parabolē, the Greek word that translates the Hebrew mashal, which can mean a proverb, a riddle or a story. A mashal invites the hearer to work, and the saying about those who see without seeing, quoted from Isaiah 6:9, is Isaiah's own comment on a message that can be heard without being received.

In the boat the disciples call Jesus epistata, 'Master,' a title that Luke alone uses of Him, and they say it twice: 'Master, Master, we are perishing,' apollymetha. When Jesus acts He epetimēsen, 'rebuked,' the wind and the water. It is the verb Luke has used for Jesus' command to unclean spirits, Luke 4:35, and to a fever, Luke 4:39. The sea is treated as an enemy to be spoken to, a detail that fits the Old Testament idea of the raging waters as a hostile force that God alone can stop. Their question is tis ara houtos estin, 'Who then is this?', with ara suggesting that they are working out a conclusion that is bigger than they expected.

With Legion, the name is the Latin legiōn, and the demons ask not to be sent into the abyssos, the 'Abyss,' the deep place of confinement. Luke's remark that the healed man was 'sitting at Jesus' feet, clothed and in his right mind,' verse 35, uses the verb sōphroneō for sanity, 'in his right mind,' a word that means sound-minded self-control. The man begins by being named for his army of occupiers and ends by being sent to tell what God has done, and Luke has him proclaim 'how much Jesus had done for him,' so that the God of verse 39 and the Jesus of verse 39 are one.

The verb sōzō, 'save, heal, rescue,' links the whole movement. The healed man 'was healed,' esōthē, verse 36, the woman's faith 'has healed you,' sesōken, verse 48, and Jairus is promised that his daughter 'will be healed,' sōthēsetai, verse 50. English separates healing and saving, but Luke does not. The woman who touches the kraspedon, the fringe of His cloak, receives a physical cure and is publicly called 'daughter,' thygatēr, so that the Lord restores her place in the community along with her body. Finally, His words to the dead girl, hē pais egeire, 'Child, arise,' use the verb of resurrection, egeirō, and the parents are 'astounded,' exestēsan, a word of being beside oneself.

typology.type: The Lord who rules the raging sea, Psalms 89 and 107
typology.fulfillment: The Psalms describe the LORD as the one who stills the waves, 'You rule the raging sea,' Psalm 89:9, and 'He calmed the storm to a whisper,' Psalm 107:29. In Luke 8 the disciples do not quote the psalms, but their question, 'Who is this?', is their dawning discovery that the person in the boat is doing what only the LORD does. The correspondence is that the rescue comes by a word. The escalation is that the God of the psalm hears a cry from afar, whereas here He is in the boat, asleep and then awake. The type falls short in that the psalm tells of sailors saved by a distant God, and the Gospel tells of a God who joins them in the storm.

Isaiah promised that God's word, like rain on the soil, would not come back without fruit. The sower parable puts that promise into a field and shows the word falling on four kinds of ground. The correspondence is that God's word really does bear fruit, a hundredfold in verse 8, a figure that recalls Isaac's harvest in Genesis 26:12 where the LORD blessed him. The escalation is that the Sower is also the Word incarnate, John 1:14, so the seed and the One who sows are not separate. The type falls short in that Isaiah's picture does not explain why the word sometimes fails to take root, and Jesus' parable supplies exactly that.

typology.type: Raising the child, the pattern of Elijah and Elisha
typology.fulfillment: Elijah and Elisha each restored a child to a mother, 1 Kings 17:17 to 24 and 2 Kings 4:32 to 37, after prayer and bodily effort. Jairus' daughter is raised with the simplest possible act, Jesus taking her by the hand and saying 'Child, get up!' The correspondence is the return of a dead child to waiting parents. The escalation is in the means, for Jesus does not pray first and does not labour. The type falls short as a picture of final resurrection, because the child would die again, and Jesus, who calls her sleep, anticipates the day when death itself will be undone, 1 Corinthians 15:26.

typology.type: The unclean made clean, the fringe and the flow of blood
typology.fulfillment: Under Leviticus 15 a woman with a long flow of blood passed uncleanness to what she touched. The Torah expects the clean to be defiled by the unclean. In this story the direction reverses: she touches the tassel on Jesus' cloak, the very thing Numbers 15:38 to 39 said would remind Israel of God's commands, and the result is that she is healed and He is not defiled. The correspondence is the law's concern for holiness; the escalation is that holiness in Jesus is stronger than impurity. The picture falls short in that it is a healing and not yet a cleansing from sin, which comes by His death, Hebrews 9:13 to 14.

study.christ:
The question the disciples ask in verse 25 is the question the whole chapter presses on the reader, and the answer is more than a title. The chapter shows Christ as the Lord of the word: the one who sows it, explains it, and by implication stands behind it. He speaks of 'the word of God' as the seed, and yet in Luke it is also His word, as when He says in 6:47 that someone 'comes to Me and hears My words.' The family He calls His own in verse 21 are those who 'hear the word of God and carry it out,' and Luke 11:28 repeats it. To be near to Jesus is to be a doer of that word. This is a startling thing for a teacher to say about his own mother and brothers.

He is Lord of creation. The sea obeys Him as it obeys the LORD in Psalm 89:9. A very old strand of Old Testament thought regarded the sea as chaos and danger, and the Creator alone could set its limits, Job 38:8 to 11. Jesus does not ask for the sea to be calmed; He tells it to be calm, and in that act He takes up God's own prerogative. The disciples were not sure what they had in the boat with them, and Luke leaves the question open for the reader's answer.

He is Lord over evil. Even Legion recognises Him as 'Jesus, Son of the Most High God,' verse 28, before the disciples have worked out who He is. The demons' knowledge is accurate and useless; they know who He is and beg for mercy. The healed man, in contrast, is sent as a witness.

He is the one who bears no uncleanness. The tombs, the pigs, the flow of blood and the corpse are all things which in the law made a person unclean, and Jesus meets all four without being defiled. This is the pattern of the gospel in miniature. He takes what is impure and makes it whole, and ultimately the cost of that will be borne in His own body on the cross, where He bears the curse, Galatians 3:13.

And He is the Lord of life. 'She is not dead but asleep' is not denial; the crowd knew she was dead, and Jesus is describing death from the vantage of one who can wake the sleeper. Paul uses the same idiom of believers who have died, 1 Thessalonians 4:14. Jairus' daughter is a sign of the day when He will call, and the dead will hear.

A word of caution about allegory. The pigs, the number of the demons or the exact kind of soil are not hidden code for church history. Jesus Himself interprets the sower, and the reading should stay within what He says. The line to Christ is clear without invention: He is the Sower, the Word and the Lord, and in each scene the one who has no one else to turn to turns to Him and is not turned away.
study.god:
The chapter shows God as the one whose word is the power behind everything. In the parable the seed is 'the word of God,' and the miracles show that same word in action: 'He commands even the winds and the water, and they obey Him.' There is a unity here. The God who speaks seeds into hearts is the God whose speech stills storms, and the two kinds of speech are not separate powers. His word can be refused, as the first three soils show, but it cannot be exhausted or overruled.

It shows God as sovereign over the things people fear most. The sea, the demons, a disease no physician could cure, and death itself are not independent forces with their own authority. This matters in a world where each of them has a claim to be the final fact. The chapter teaches that none of them is. Each yields, not after a struggle, but at once, and that is what it means to say that God is God.

It also shows God's mercy to the overlooked. He allows the Gerasene man to be sent home as a missionary, though the people of his own town begged Jesus to leave. He stops in a pressing crowd to find the woman who has touched Him, which is surprising given that the healing had already happened. The purpose of the question appears in verse 47: she is brought out of hiding so that she can be named as a daughter and so that her healing is not a theft. God's dealing with her is public, personal and restorative, which is a different thing from a mere cure.

It shows God's strange timing. Jairus' daughter dies while Jesus is delayed by the woman. The messenger says, 'Your daughter is dead. Do not bother the Teacher anymore.' God does not hurry to rescue the child before she dies. He lets her die, and then He raises her. This does not make the delay less painful, but it tells us that the Lord is not ruled by the clock or defeated by it. His answer to hopelessness is not an explanation but a word, 'Do not be afraid; just believe.'

There is a doctrine here about the holiness of God as well. The demons plead not to be sent into the Abyss, which shows they know that there is a judgment, and Jesus does not hide that evil has a limit. The people of the region respond to His power with fear and want Him gone, and He goes. God does not force Himself on those who will not have Him, though He leaves a witness behind.

For worship, the chapter calls us to a trust that does not wait for calm. The disciples woke Him and He was there. The woman reached out in secret and was heard. The father believed past the point of evidence. Our worship should include the cry 'we are perishing' as well as the song of those who are safe, since the Lord of Luke 8 answers both.

crossReferences.note: God's word is likened to rain and snow that water the earth and give seed to the sower, and it will not return empty. The parable of the sower is the same picture seen from the side of the soil. The promise guarantees that the word accomplishes its purpose, and the parable explains why that purpose is sometimes seen only in some hearers.

The prophet is told to go and speak to a people who will be 'ever hearing, but never understanding.' Jesus quotes this to explain why parables conceal as well as reveal. It frames the parable's first three soils as a replay of Isaiah's day, and it keeps hope alive for the hearer who turns.

Sailors in a tempest, their courage melted, cry out to the LORD, and He calms the storm to a whisper and guides them to harbour. Luke 8:22 to 25 is almost a retelling, with one difference that matters: the Lord who answers the cry is the one sleeping in the boat.

A single line declares that the LORD rules the raging sea and stills its waves. When Jesus rebukes the wind and the waters, the disciples are watching something Israel's worshippers had assigned to God alone. Their question 'Who is this?' is the beginning of the right answer.

Another storm, another sleeper in the hold, another frightened crew who wake him. The captain asks 'How can you sleep?' and asks the sleeper to call on his God. The contrast shows Jesus is not Jonah. Jonah is asleep in flight from God, and the storm is aimed at him, but Jesus sleeps in trust and is Himself the answer to the storm.

A woman with a long flow of blood is unclean for as long as it lasts. This is the legal background to the woman in verse 43, who has lived under it for twelve years. It explains why she approaches secretly and trembling, and why Jesus' public affirmation of her restores more than her health.

Israelites are to wear tassels on their garments with a blue cord so that they will remember and obey God's commands. The fringe the woman grasps is this tassel. The detail may be incidental, but it places her hand on the visible reminder of the law at the very moment the Lawgiver heals her.

Isaac sowed in the land and 'that very year he reaped a hundredfold,' with the LORD's blessing. The hundredfold of Luke 8:8 is the same figure, so the good soil is not a modest success but a harvest of blessing.

Elijah, praying, restores the widow's son to life and gives him back to his mother. This is the pattern that sets the scene for Jairus' daughter, and the difference is in the style of action: Elijah calls on the LORD three times and Jesus simply says, 'Child, get up!'

'Be doers of the word, and not hearers only.' James states the application of the parable of the sower and Jesus' redefinition of family in verse 21. Hearing the word and doing it are not two stages but one response, and the failure to do it is self-deception.

study.oneStory:
From the start of the Bible the world is made by speech. 'God said' stands at the head of every creative act in Genesis 1, and Psalm 33:9 says that He spoke and it came to be. Luke 8 shows the same voice, now in Galilee. The seed that falls on the soil is the creative word entering a ruined field, and the command that stills the sea is the word that once set the waters within bounds. When the creation fell, the word was refused, and one of the lasting results is the sort of heart the first three soils describe.

Israel's own story added questions to the first answer. Why does the word not always bear fruit? Isaiah said that hearts could be hardened, and the history of the kings and the exile gave plenty of examples. But Isaiah also promised that the word would accomplish what God pleased, and that a day would come when the deaf would hear. Luke 8 offers the first half of that tension and the beginnings of the second. The sower sows anyway, and some of the seed takes.

The scenes that follow are the signs of the kingdom pressing back against the curse. Chaos is rebuked, the demonic is cast out, the diseased are healed, and the dead are raised. Each is a small restoration of something Genesis 3 broke. These are samples of a creation being put right, not the full renewal, since in Luke's story the sea will rise again and the girl will one day die. But the pattern is established: when the Word meets disorder, disorder gives way.

The cross and resurrection will give the pattern its foundation. The One who tells the dead girl to rise will be Himself raised, and His rising is 'the firstfruits of those who have fallen asleep,' 1 Corinthians 15:20, using the very idiom of sleep that He used of her. The Gerasene man commissioned to tell what God had done is the first of the missionaries to the Gentiles that Acts will multiply, and the women who funded the mission are the first to bring news of the empty tomb.

The new creation completes the chapter. In Revelation the sea is gone, Revelation 21:1, and death is no more, Revelation 21:4. The storm that terrified fishermen will not be calmed again and again, because it will not be there. The word that was heard with endurance will have produced its harvest, and the people who held it fast will live in the world it made. Every person Jesus restores in Luke 8 is a promise that the whole creation will be restored in the same way, and by the same voice.

sermon.title: The Parable of the Sower
sermon.why: From Begg's series A Study in Luke, this message on Luke 8 opens the parable of the sower, showing how the same word meets different hearts and how only the good soil that receives and holds the word bears lasting fruit. A faithful, expository handling of the teaching that anchors this movement.

quiz.q: According to the parable of the sower, what determines whether the word bears fruit?

options.text: The condition of the heart that hears it, since the good soil hears, holds on, and perseveres.
options.note: Luke 8:15 makes the receptive, persevering heart the good soil that bears a crop.

options.text: How joyfully a person first receives the word.
options.note: The rocky soil received it with joy yet had no root; initial joy is not enough without perseverance.

options.text: The quality or strength of the seed being sown.
options.note: The seed, the word of God, is always good; the difference lies in the soil, not the seed.

options.text: Whether the sower scatters the seed skillfully.
options.note: The parable focuses on the soils, not the sower's technique.

quiz.q: Who did Jesus say His true mother and brothers are?

options.text: Those who hear the word of God and carry it out.
options.note: Luke 8:21 defines Jesus' family by hearing and doing God's word.

options.text: Those who listen carefully to the word of God.
options.note: Hearing is essential, but Jesus adds 'and carry it out'; doing completes it.

options.text: His biological mother and brothers who came to see Him.
options.note: They prompted the saying, but Jesus redefined family around obedience to the word.

options.text: The crowds who gathered to watch His miracles.
options.note: Mere spectators are not His family; hearing and doing the word is the mark.

quiz.q: What did the calming of the storm reveal about Jesus?

options.text: That He is Lord even over wind and water, doing what Scripture ascribes to God alone.
options.note: The disciples' question in Luke 8:25 recognizes an authority that belongs to God.

options.text: That He could protect His disciples from danger.
options.note: True, but the deeper revelation is His divine authority over creation itself.

options.text: That the storm happened to die down when He awoke.
options.note: It was no coincidence; Jesus rebuked the wind and waters and they obeyed.

options.text: That the disciples had nothing to fear from nature at all.
options.note: The point is not that nature is harmless but that Jesus commands it.

quiz.q: Why did Jesus ask 'Who touched Me?' in the crowd?

options.text: To draw the healed woman's hidden faith into the open and send her away in peace.
options.note: Luke 8:47-48 shows Jesus bringing her trembling faith to public confession and assurance.

options.text: To distinguish real faith from the crowd merely pressing against Him.
options.note: A true observation, but the fuller aim was to draw her out and give her peace, not only to make a distinction.

options.text: Because He did not actually know who had touched Him.
options.note: Jesus knew power had gone out from Him; He asked to draw the woman out, not from ignorance.

options.text: To rebuke the woman for touching Him while unclean.
options.note: He does not rebuke her; He calls her Daughter and commends her faith.

quiz.q: What did Jesus tell Jairus when news came that his daughter had died?

options.text: Do not be afraid; just believe, and she will be healed.
options.note: Luke 8:50 records Jesus' call to faith in the face of death.

options.text: It is too late now, but her death is not the end.
options.note: Death was indeed not the end, but Jesus' actual word was a summons to believe, not resignation.

options.text: That nothing more could be done for the girl.
options.note: The opposite; Jesus went on to raise her, calling Jairus to believe.

options.text: That Jairus should have brought Him sooner.
options.note: Jesus offers no reproach, only a call to trust Him.

questions: Jesus says the same word falls on every kind of heart. Which soil best describes how you have been receiving God's word lately, and what would it take to become good soil that holds on and perseveres?
The thorns are the worries, riches, and pleasures of life that choke the word. Which of these is most likely to crowd out God's word in your life right now?
In the storm Jesus asked, 'Where is your faith?' When fear rises, where do you tend to lose sight of who is in the boat with you?

The bleeding woman reached out in trembling, secret faith, and Jesus drew her into the open and called her Daughter. Is there a place where you need to bring your quiet faith, or your shame, honestly to Him?
To a grieving father Jesus said, do not be afraid, only believe. Where is Jesus calling you to trust Him in a situation that looks, humanly, already lost?

translationNotes.note: The words 'though seeing, they may not see' quote Isaiah 6:9; parables both reveal the kingdom to the receptive and veil it from the hard of heart.
Manuscripts vary between Gerasenes, Gadarenes, and Gergesenes for the region across the lake; the BSB follows Gerasenes, all naming the largely Gentile territory east of Galilee.
The word rendered 'healed you' is the same Greek verb elsewhere translated 'saved you'; Jesus' healing of the body points to the fuller salvation received by faith.
